message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Customer Churn Analysis: Residential Broadband, H1 2026
Customer Insight Team, Brightline Fibre, July 2026

1. Purpose
This analysis examines residential broadband churn in the first half of 2026, identifies where it is concentrated, and recommends where retention spending should be focused in H2. Churn is our largest single driver of revenue loss and acquisition cost: each lost customer costs around £180 to replace through marketing and installation.

2. Context
Brightline applied an annual price rise of 6.5% to all residential broadband customers in April 2026, in line with the terms of their contracts. Two national competitors launched aggressive introductory offers in the same quarter. Our minimum contract term for new customers is 18 months; after that, customers roll onto a monthly contract at the same price and can leave with 30 days' notice.

Churn in this analysis means customers whose broadband service ended during the period. Customers who moved to another Brightline product, such as a business or mobile-bundle tariff, and customers who moved home and transferred their service within our network, are not counted as churn. Customer numbers are taken from the billing system at 1 January.

3. Churn by contract status
Table 1. Residential broadband churn, 1 January to 30 June 2026
Segment | Customers at 1 January | Churned in H1 | H1 churn rate
In minimum term | 182,000 | 5,460 | 3.0%
Out of contract, less than 12 months | 64,000 | 7,040 | 11.0%
Out of contract, 12 months or more | 48,000 | 3,840 | 8.0%
Total | 294,000 | 16,340 | 5.6%

Churn is low among customers in their minimum term, as expected, because leaving early incurs a charge. Once out of contract, churn rises sharply. It is highest among our longest-standing out-of-contract customers, those who have been out of contract for 12 months or more, who appear to accumulate dissatisfaction with paying full price over time.

Table 2. Reasons given at cancellation (H1 2026, where recorded)
Reason | Share
Price / found a cheaper deal | 46%
Moving home | 21%
Service reliability | 14%
Customer service experience | 9%
Other | 10%

Price was the dominant reason, cited by almost half of leavers. Cancellations peaked in May, the month after the price rise, when 3,620 customers left, compared with a monthly average of about 2,540 in the rest of the half-year.

4. Revenue impact
Average revenue per customer is £34 a month. The 16,340 customers lost in H1 therefore represent annualised revenue of about £7.4 million, before the cost of replacing them.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Target a proactive retention offer at customers who have been out of contract for 12 months or more, since this is where churn is highest. The offer would be a 10% discount in return for a new 12-month commitment. There are 48,000 such customers, and the discount would cost about £2.0 million a year if all accepted; in practice we expect take-up of around 40%.
5.2 Review the timing and communication of future annual price rises. The spike in cancellations after the 8% April price rise suggests that customers were not adequately prepared, and that clearer advance communication could reduce price-driven churn.
5.3 Investigate the reliability complaints, which are concentrated in three exchange areas.
5.4 Report churn monthly by segment to the Commercial Committee from September, so that the effect of the retention offer can be tracked.

6. Conclusion
Churn is concentrated among long-standing out-of-contract customers and is primarily price-driven. A targeted retention offer to this group, together with better price-rise communication, is the most effective use of our H2 retention budget.
</document>
response:
# Review: Customer Churn Analysis, H1 2026

The arithmetic in Table 1 is sound, but the document's main finding is contradicted by its own data. That finding drives the headline recommendation, so it needs fixing before this circulates.

## Errors that change the conclusions

**1. The highest-churn segment is misidentified (Section 3, 5.1, 6).**
The text says churn is highest among customers out of contract for 12 months or more. Table 1 shows the opposite:

| Segment | H1 churn rate |
|---|---|
| Out of contract, <12 months | **11.0%** |
| Out of contract, 12+ months | 8.0% |

The "accumulated dissatisfaction over time" explanation is therefore explaining something that isn't in the data. Recommendation 5.1 and the conclusion both target the wrong group. The <12-month group (64,000 customers) also has more leavers in absolute terms (7,040 vs 3,840). Retargeting the offer would raise its cost: a 10% discount on £34/month is about £40.80 per customer per year, so about £2.6m if all 64,000 accepted, or about £1.0m at 40% take-up. Take-up and cost should be re-estimated for this group.

**2. The revenue figure is overstated (Section 4).**
16,340 × £34 × 12 = about **£6.7m**, not £7.4m. Either the figure or the underlying assumptions (a different ARPU, or a different churn count) need correcting. The replacement cost (16,340 × £180, about £2.9m) could also be stated, since Section 1 raises it.

**3. The price rise is quoted inconsistently.**
Section 2 says 6.5%, but Recommendation 5.2 says 8%. One of them is wrong, and it matters because 5.2 builds its argument on the size of the rise.

## Weaker reasoning

- **Section 5.2 attributes the May spike to poor communication.** The document itself notes that two competitors launched aggressive offers in the same quarter. The spike can't be assigned to the price rise, or to its communication, without separating out the competitor effect. For example, compare reasons given by May leavers against other months, or look at which competitors customers moved to.
- **Section 5.1 doesn't consider discount leakage.** A 10% discount is also given to customers who would have stayed anyway. A break-even comparison would help: the discount cost vs. the saved churn at £180 replacement cost plus retained revenue.
- **The reasons data is partial.** Table 2 is "where recorded", and the coverage rate isn't given. Please state it. "Primarily price-driven" is also a plurality (46%), not a majority.
- **Section 5.3 has no supporting evidence.** The "three exchange areas" claim has no data behind it. Please name the exchanges and give complaint or churn figures.
- **Segment definitions need clarifying.** Segments are fixed at 1 January, so customers who moved from in-term to out-of-contract during H1 are classed as in-term. Customers who joined during H1 are excluded from the denominator. Both are reasonable choices, but they should be stated.

## Minor points

- Section 5.4 proposes monthly reporting "from September". The document is dated July, and it is now November, so the start date and the offer's rollout timeline need updating.
- The 40% take-up assumption has no source.

## What checks out

- Table 1 totals: 294,000 customers, 16,340 churned, and 5.6% overall are all correct, as are the segment rates.
- Table 2 sums to 100%.
- The May average (about 2,540 for the other five months) matches the totals.
- The £2.0m cost in 5.1 is right for 48,000 customers at a 10% discount, though that is the wrong population.

## Suggested next step

Rewrite Sections 3, 5.1, and 6 around the <12-month out-of-contract group, correct the revenue figure and the 6.5%/8% inconsistency, and add a competitor-effect caveat to 5.2. I can make those edits if you share the file.
